mission_3.prediction: I inspected the open and constrained maps. I changed the influence distance for social_1 from 1.00 m to 0.20 m, keeping the repulsion strength at 0.70 and the step at 0.08. Both social_1 and social_2 showed succeeded with a complete preview path. On both maps the baseline, social_1 and social_2 lines lie on top of each other, so the path stayed the same and did not move farther from the person. The 0.20 m influence circle only just surrounds the person, so repulsion was zero along the route, and the refined path matched the original.
mission_3.comparison: For A*, the completed condition with the largest minimum person clearance was the baseline at 0.742 m, with 0.8 s inside the personal space threshold. social_1 gave 0.734 m and 1.4 s, and social_2 gave 0.724 m and 1.5 s, so the field did not improve either measure and the differences are tiny. Time and distance barely changed, at 46.2 s and 13.17 m for the baseline against 46.7 s and 13.20 m for social_2, so there was no real cost. For RRT, the largest clearance was social_2 at 1.735 m, against 1.706 m for the baseline, with 0 s in personal space for all three conditions. It was no slower, at 43.7 s against 43.8 s, with a distance of 11.57 m against 11.59 m. RRT’s route already passed far outside the influence distance, so the field had nothing to push against, and the 0.03 m gain is within normal variation.
mission_3.recommendation: I would keep RRT with social_2, which succeeded with a minimum person clearance of 1.735 m, 0 s in personal space, and an execution time of 43.7 s over 11.57 m. Compared with the alternative, A* baseline, which succeeded with a clearance of 0.742 m, 0.8 s inside the personal space threshold and a time of 46.2 s, RRT kept more than twice the distance from the person and was also faster. The advantage mostly comes from RRT’s randomly sampled route, not from the field, since the planned length did not change with the condition. RRT also passed closer to the walls, with a static clearance of 0.15 to 0.18 m against about 0.6 m for A*, which is a trade-off I would check before deploying. These static-person trials cannot tell us how the robot handles a moving person, such as someone stepping into the path, how quickly it must react, or whether it can predict where the person is heading. They also cover one trial per condition, so they don’t show how reliable the choice is.
